en: ‘If fortune favors you, Akshumkar left by your father
Will come to meet you,’ she said.
It is Akshumkar itself!
Surely for me
That dear creature has been grieving.”
When he saw Akshumkar,
It was as though his father Manas, this very day,
Had come alive again beside him,
As though God had granted his wish.
When he saw Akshumkar,
Bracing his right side,
“My formidable father!” he wept.
Bracing his left side,
“My protector, my father!” he wept.
“The rushing place of two rivers—
My khan father, like the stillness where they meet!
Where two mountains meet,
My khan father, like their rocky ridge!”
Seeing Akshumkar, he cried aloud,
Called out his khan father Manas's name,
As though he had seen his fierce-maned father Manas.
Tears streamed from his eyes in all directions.
He could not even stop his running nose.
The boy could not wipe his tears.
When sorrow strikes, the heart
Cannot stay still: it breaks apart.
The poor orphan boy left by Manas—
His tears kept pouring out.
When he fell behind, Akshumkar
Called loudly from the sky
And above that boy
Circled, flashing bright.
When the boy drew near,
My dear Akshumkar
Flew smoothly on, flashing bright.
Meeting Akshumkar,
What had broken was joined again,
What had scattered was gathered.
The orphan left by Manas—
His life, frail as a fly, rejoiced.
What he had lost was found.
Thus his honor was restored.
Weeping, his eyes burned like coals.
To see Akshumkar,
He watched with all his longing.
Walking straight on in distress,
To God, whose command surpasses all,
The boy prayed in supplication.
Akshumkar was found among the cliffs.
Thus the boy's honor was restored:
His inheritance from his father Manas.
It was Akshumkar itself.
When Semetey looked closely—
May I be sacrificed to Allah!—
Akshumkar's young
Still had wing feathers like needles.
It had brooded diligently and brought forth a bird.
Behold the good fortune God granted:
He had brought him to Akshumkar.
“It is a bird I can take with me.
Ah, this world!
It is a possession left by my father Manas.
The Akshumkar my mother spoke of—
It is Akshumkar itself.
Almighty Allah, the one God,
Has chosen this time to bring us together!”
He banished all his sorrow.
The orphan put aside his grief.
May I be sacrificed to Allah!
Appearing from the unseen,
A gray two-year-old wether came down.
Semetey slaughtered the gray wether and laid it out.
He performed a rite for Akshumkar,
Smearing its limbs with fat.
Clairvoyant until death,
Plain-spoken besides,
Both a discerning judge and a lion,
Akshumkar's young
He examined there.
The morning-star hero left by Manas,
When he looked at it sideways,
Akshumkar's young
Had the form of a merlin.
“It is truly a mighty hunting bird,” he thought.
The orphan left by Manas—
His heart was stirred by it.
When he looked from either side,
It had the form of a hobby.
When he looked along its edges,
Oh, dear Akshumkar,
How wondrous it was!
It had the form of a sparrowhawk.
Its talons were iron, its jess-clasp bronze,
It measured two ells around.
Black eyes and powerful gray legs,
It would let no prey it saw escape,
Never draw back from what it saw.
It would leave none of a platterful of food,
Never draw back once it sprang.
It would spread its wings without a shriek.
My dear creature,
Nor would it let a goose take flight from the lake.
It would draw in its tail without a shriek.
If it lived and grew to maturity,
My dear creature would let no swan fly from the lake.
“It is a bird left by my fierce-maned father Manas.
My fierce mother Kanykei—
This is what she spoke of.”
Seeing it, the young hero made ready.
The orphan's heart was satisfied and joyful.
The orphan boy traveled on again,
Preparing to go farther toward Talas.
“My dear broad Talas,
Where my father, Khan Manas, dwelt!
Dear land where my father lived,
Junipers and birches mingled—
My wretched head is distraught.
When my father Manas was alive,
The Argyn and Kyrgyz turned toward its lowlands
And made their home here.
Kymyz by day and girls by night—
Such had been the life here.
More rice than coarse grain,
More silver than tin,
More foxes than gray hares,
Much wealth gathered at the threshold!
Is this not the finest land?
Would not its inhabitants find peace?”
Deeply stirred, the orphan traveled on.
Traveling on, the orphan grew excited.
A mighty, powerful flowing river,
The broad Talas, he came upon.
The waters of Talas had swollen,
Risen over the tops of the rocks.
The waters of Urbus had poured into it.
A flood swept over its surface.
Stones rattled upon its bed,
Foam glittered above,
Heaving and breaking apart,
It poured in waves like camel humps.
When you looked downstream,
It seemed like four great rivers.
Pines fell and rafts drifted,
Birches and willows floated past.
The cliff face was stripped away.
Young firs and pines
Were torn up by the roots
And hurled against the bank.
The person watching it
Felt his entrusted life shrivel with fear.
“When she told me her tale,
My wise mother said this:
‘If you meet a swollen river,
Do not fret and search for a ford.
Go straight into it,’ she said.
The reason I may go straight in:
My forefathers were all khans,
Blessed by Kydyr from their very roots.
All my earliest ancestors were khans,
Blessed by Kydyr from the beginning.
My own father passed as a sovereign.
Not merely from running water—my father
Never drew back even from death.
Not merely from a swollen river—my father
Never retreated from a man.
His protector, Kozhosan,
Will protect me! My mother said so.
My support is the forty chiltens.
If they will support me, now is the time.
If God sets my affairs right,
He is a lion whose protector lives.
If my generous father protects me,
From this flowing, speechless enemy
How could I draw back in fear?
Let the angel Gabriel say,
‘If he crosses, I shall take his soul,’
And stand ready to do it:
Why should I turn back from him?
Does not a mortal man die?
What Allah lays upon his head,
Must not this entrusted life endure?
Will not the dug grave receive him?
The eighteen thousand worlds—
The black earth swallows them up.
Before this surging water,
I shall not hesitate upon the road.
Whether I die or live,
I entrust myself to You: God, protect me!”
(His father Manas the Lion
Never turned back from flowing water,
Never shrank a hair's breadth from death.)
Brave Semen, who took after his father,
Into that flowing water,
Crying “Go!” brave Semen plunged.
Urging Aktulpar onward,
Breaking down the edge of the bank,
He entered the flashing water.
The forty chiltens, his protectors,
Took him under the arms and supported him.
A dark-spotted leopard
Raged beside his flank.
The spiritual protectors of Khan Manas
Joined in supporting him.
A short-tailed, gray-maned lion,
Pressing close and making ready,
Supported him at his side.
Had not the saintly one foretold it?
His mother's words were these:
‘When God chooses to grant His favor,
Khan Manas's forty companions
Will support you through the water.’
Such had been her prediction.
When he looked to his right,
Riding the horse Ai-sarala,
Its horsehair tail tied tightly,
A red face, a radiant countenance,
Tall of stature, broad of shoulder—
Both a mighty wrestler and a lion,
As vast as half a mountain,
As though he would devour anyone he met,
Wearing yellow leather trousers,
Holding a spear without a tuft,
A bare sword fastened at his side,
Brown-eyed, with no trace of gray,
White-faced, without a freckle,
Girded with a golden belt,
His moon-like face touched by light,
Girded with a silver belt,
Smiling yet solemn,
His sun-like face touched by light,
Cleansed of the dark faith,
Who fled the unbelievers and became their stranger,
Who killed his own father,
Who brought his tongue to the profession of faith,
Who raised rebellion against the Khagan,
The golden throne he had occupied
He renounced and cast aside.
When they went on campaign against the Khagan,
With my khan father Manas among them,
When they unleashed great turmoil,
In the Khagan's Great Beijing,
Along the edge of Middle Beijing,
Beside Chong-Mazar,
On the ridge of Kyz-Korgon,
He had his banner unfurled.
They campaigned against the Khagan,
Fought six months without fleeing.
The massed Chinese and many Kalmaks,
They broke through the frontiers.
Four great divisions of troops drawn from the Sarts,
Having their dutars played,
By Kojozhash, son of Karazhoi—
Deceived by the Chinese—
His head was shattered by a shot.
The noble warrior who died a martyr,
Almam the Lion, who died in the Khagan's land,
